title: حِكَايَةُ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ مَعَ شَمْسِ النَّهَارِ
titleEn: ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār
part: Night 163 · ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 791–795 (Night 163, continuing directly from nights-162), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 163 continues the tale of ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and Shams al-Nahār. In the morning Shams al-Nahār's slave-girl comes to the jeweller; he persuades her that his own house is safer than the palace, and her mistress agrees. He refuses the purse she sends, furnishes his second house richly, and brings ʿAlī there. At nightfall Shams al-Nahār arrives with two maids; the lovers faint in each other's arms, then eat, drink, and she sings to the lute. In the midst of their joy a little maid runs in: the house is surrounded. The jeweller leaps into a neighbour's house and hides till midnight, fearing the Caliph has found them out. The neighbour tells him it was the thieves who robbed the street the day before: they have stripped his house and, he says, killed his guests; they have killed men of the Caliph's household too, and the watch are hunting them. Fearing above all for the lovers' secret, the jeweller goes home. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّالِثَةُ وَالسِّتُّونَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thālithatu wa-al-sittūna baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the third-and-sixty after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and sixty-third night,
sentences.n: The heading is built as before: al-thālitha, “the third”, feminine to agree with layla; then wa-al-sittūn, “and the sixty”; then baʿda al-miʾa, “after the hundred”.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الْجَوْهَرِيَّ قَالَ فَأَقَمْتُ عِنْدَهُ تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ أُسَامِرُهُ إِلَى أَنْ طَلَعَ النَّهَارُ ثُمَّ صَلَّيْتُ الصُّبْحَ وَخَرَجْتُ مِنْ عِنْدِهِ وَذَهَبْتُ إِلَي مَنْزِلِي
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-jawhariyya qāla fa-aqamtu ʿindahu tilka al-laylata usāmiruhu ilā an ṭalaʿa al-nahāru thumma ṣallaytu al-ṣubḥa wa-kharajtu min ʿindihi wa-dhahabtu ilā manzilī
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the jeweller said: So I-stayed with-him that night, keeping-night-company-with-him, until the day rose; then I-prayed the dawn (prayer), and went-out from with-him, and went to my-dwelling.
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the jeweller said: I stayed with him all that night, talking with him until the day broke. Then I prayed the dawn prayer, took my leave of him, and went home.
sentences.n: tilka al-laylata, accusative of time, “(throughout) that night”. usāmiruhu, Form III of samar, “to keep someone company in talk by night”, a circumstantial clause with no wa-: “conversing with him”. ilā an, “until”. al-ṣubḥ, “the dawn”, here the dawn prayer. The shadda of صلّيت is the print's own. The print spells ilā with ي here (الي), after الى a line earlier; it is read ilā all the same.

sentences.t: فَمَا اسْتَقَرَّيْتُ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا حَتَّى جَاءَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ فَسَلَّمَتْ عَلَيَّ فَرَدَدْتُ عَلَيْهَا السَّلَامَ وَحَدَّثْتُهَا بِمَا كَانَ بَيْنِي وَبَيْنَ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ
sentences.tr: fa-mā istaqarraytu illā qalīlan ḥattā jāʾati al-jāriyatu fa-sallamat ʿalayya fa-radadtu ʿalayhā al-salāma wa-ḥaddathtuhā bi-mā kāna baynī wa-bayna ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin
sentences.l: And I-had- not -settled except a-little until the slave-girl came, and she-greeted me, and I-returned to-her the greeting, and told-her of what had-been between-me and between ʿAlī son of Bakkār.
sentences.i: I had scarcely settled down when the slave-girl came. She greeted me and I returned her greeting, and I told her all that had passed between me and ʿAlī ibn Bakkār.
sentences.n: istaqarraytu, “I settled, came to rest”, is a Middle Arabic form: the doubled verb istaqarra is conjugated as though its last root letter were y, where Classical has istaqrartu. The shadda is the print's own, as are those of الّا and عليّ. mā … illā qalīlan ḥattā, “I had not (stayed) but a little before …”. sallama ʿalā, “to greet”; radda ʿalā al-salām, “to return the greeting”. ḥaddatha bi-, “to tell about”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ اعْلَمْ أَنَّ الْخَلِيفَةَ تَوَجَّهَ مِنْ عِنْدِنَا وَأَنَّ مَجْلِسَنَا لَا أَحَدَ فِيهِ وَهُوَ أَسْتَرُلَنَا وَأَحْسَنُ
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-jāriyatu iʿlam anna al-khalīfata tawajjaha min ʿindinā wa-anna majlisanā lā aḥada fīhi wa-huwa astaru lanā wa-aḥsanu
sentences.l: And the slave-girl said: Know that the Caliph has-set-off from with-us, and that our-sitting-place, no one (is) in-it, and it (is) more-concealing for-us and better.
sentences.i: The slave-girl said, “You should know that the Caliph has gone away from us, and there is no one in our apartments; that would be safer for us, and better.”
sentences.n: tawajjaha (Form V), “to set out, turn one's face towards”; its shadda is the print's own. lā aḥada fīhi, “there is no one in it”, the lā that denies a whole class. astaru, an elative of satara, “to veil”: “more sheltering, more discreet”. The print runs it together with lanā, “for us”, as one word (استرلنا); the spacing is kept and the two words are read.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهَا كَلَامُكِ صَحِيحٌ وَلَكِنَّهُ لَيْسَ كَمَنْزِلِي هَذَا فَإِنَّهُ أَلْيَقُ بِنَا وَأَسْتَرُلَنَا
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahā kalāmuki ṣaḥīḥun wa-lākinnahu laysa ka-manzilī hādhā fa-innahu alyaqu binā wa-astaru lanā
sentences.l: So I-said to-her: Your-speech (is) correct, but it is- not -like this my-dwelling, for it (is) more-fitting for-us and more-concealing for-us.
sentences.i: I said to her, “What you say is true, but it is not like this house of mine, which suits us better and hides us better.”
sentences.n: alyaqu, elative of lāqa bi-, “to befit, suit”, so alyaqu binā, “more fitting for us”. As before the print runs astaru and lanā together.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ الرَّأْيُ كَمَا تَرَاهُ أَنْتَ وَأَنَا ذَاهِبَةٌ إِلَى سَيِّدَتِي لِأُخْبِرَهَا بِمَا ذَكَرْتَ وَأَعْرِضَ عَلَيْهَا مَا قُلْتَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-jāriyatu al-raʾyu ka-mā tarāhu anta wa-anā dhāhibatun ilā sayyidatī li-ukhbirahā bi-mā dhakarta wa-aʿriḍa ʿalayhā mā qulta
sentences.l: And the slave-girl said: The judgement (is) as you see-it, you; and I (am) going to my-mistress, to-inform-her of what you-mentioned and lay-before her what you-said.
sentences.i: The slave-girl said, “It shall be as you think best. I am going to my lady now to tell her what you have proposed and put your words before her.”
sentences.n: The print has غليها, a misprint for عليها, corrected here. al-raʾyu ka-mā tarāhu anta, “the judgement is as you see it”, a polite way of deferring; the added anta stresses “you”. The hamza of الرأي is the print's own. li-ukhbirahā, li- of purpose with the subjunctive, and wa-aʿriḍa shares that subjunctive. ʿaraḍa ʿalā, “to lay before, submit to”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَامَتْ وَمَضَتْ حَتَّى دَخَلَتْ عَلَى سَيِّدَتِهَا وَعَرَضَتْ عَلَيْهَا الْكَلَامَ
sentences.tr: thumma qāmat wa-maḍat ḥattā dakhalat ʿalā sayyidatihā wa-ʿaraḍat ʿalayhā al-kalāma
sentences.l: Then she-rose and went-off until she-entered upon her-mistress, and laid-before-her the speech.
sentences.i: Then she rose and went off, and came in to her mistress and put the proposal to her.
sentences.n: dakhala ʿalā, “to go in to (someone)”, to come into a person's presence. al-kalām, “the words”, here what the jeweller had said.

sentences.t: وَعَادَتْ إِلَى مَنْزِلِي وَقَالَتْ لِي الْأَمْرُ صَارَ عَلَى مَا ذَكَرْتَهُ فَهَيِّءْ لَنَا الْمَحَلَّ وَ انْتَظِرْنَا
sentences.tr: wa-ʿādat ilā manzilī wa-qālat lī al-amru ṣāra ʿalā mā dhakartahu fa-hayyiʾ lanā al-maḥalla wa-intaẓirnā
sentences.l: And she-returned to my-dwelling and said to-me: The affair has-come-to-stand upon what you-mentioned-it; so make-ready for-us the place, and wait-for-us.
sentences.i: Then she came back to my house and said to me, “It is settled as you proposed. Make the place ready for us, and wait for us.”
sentences.n: The jeweller is telling the story in his own voice. al-amru ṣāra ʿalā mā dhakartahu, “the matter has come to stand on what you mentioned”: your plan is agreed. hayyiʾ, imperative of hayyaʾa (Form II), “to make ready”; its shadda is the print's own, and the print writes the final hamza on the line (هيّء). maḥall, “place, lodging”: the house where the lovers are to meet. The print ends its line on a lone و and sets intaẓirnā at the head of the next; the spacing is kept.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَخْرَجَتْ مِنْ جَيْبِهَا كِيسًا فِيهِ دَنَانِيرُ وَقَالَتْ لِي إِنَّ سَيِّدَتِي تُسَلِّمُ عَلَيْكَ وَتَقُولُ لَكَ خُذْ هَذَا وَاقْضِ مِنْهُ مَا يَحْتَاجُ إِلَيْهِ الْحَالُ
sentences.tr: thumma akhrajat min jaybihā kīsan fīhi danānīru wa-qālat lī inna sayyidatī tusallimu ʿalayka wa-taqūlu laka khudh hādhā wa-iqḍi minhu mā yaḥtāju ilayhi al-ḥālu
sentences.l: Then she-brought-out from her-bosom a-purse, in-it dinars, and said to-me: My-mistress greets you and says to-you: Take this and settle from-it what the situation has-need of-it.
sentences.i: Then she drew from the bosom of her dress a purse with gold pieces in it, and said, “My mistress sends you her greetings and says: Take this, and pay out of it for whatever the occasion needs.”
sentences.n: jayb, the opening of a garment at the breast, where small things were carried. kīs, “purse, bag”; fīhi danānīru, “in it dinars”, describes it. danānīr, plural of dīnār, gold coins, takes no tanwīn. sallama ʿalā, “to greet”. iqḍi, imperative of qaḍā, “to settle, pay off”; in mā yaḥtāju ilayhi al-ḥālu, “what the situation needs”, ilayhi points back to mā.

sentences.t: فَأَقْسَمْتُ أَنِّي لَا آخُذُهُ مِنْهُ شَيْأً
sentences.tr: fa-aqsamtu annī lā ākhudhuhu minhu shayʾan
sentences.l: But I-swore that-I would-not take-it, of-it a-thing.
sentences.i: But I swore I would not take a single coin of it.
sentences.n: ākhudhuhu minhu shayʾan, “take it, anything of it”: the object is given twice, first as the pronoun -hu and then as shayʾan, a doubling of speech that Classical prose would avoid. شيأ is the print's spelling of shayʾan (Classical شيئا), with its hamza seated on the alif; that hamza and the madda of آخذه are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَتْهُ الْجَارِيَةُ وَعَادَتْ إِلَى سَيِّدَتِهَا فَقَالَتْ يَاسَيِّدَتِي إِنَّهُ لَمْ يَقْبَلِ الدَّرَاهِمَ بَلْ دَفَعَهَا إِلَيَّ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhathu al-jāriyatu wa-ʿādat ilā sayyidatihā fa-qālat yā sayyidatī innahu lam yaqbali al-darāhima bal dafaʿahā ilayya
sentences.l: So the slave-girl took-it and returned to her-mistress and said: O my-mistress, he did-not accept the dirhams; rather he-pushed-them to-me.
sentences.i: So the girl took it and went back to her mistress. “My lady,” she said, “he would not accept the money; he handed it straight back to me.”
sentences.n: The purse held dinars, gold; the girl now calls its contents darāhim, “dirhams”, silver coins, the word standing loosely for “money”. yaqbali takes a helping kasra before the article. dafaʿa ilā, “to hand over to, push back to”. The print runs yā sayyidatī together (ياسيدتي); the shaddas of انّه and اليّ are its own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ لَا بَأْسَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat lā baʾsa
sentences.l: So she-said: No harm.
sentences.i: “No matter,” she said.
sentences.n: lā baʾsa, “there is no harm”: the lā that denies a whole class, its noun accusative without tanwīn. The print writes بأس without its hamza (باس).

sentences.t: قَالَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ ثُمَّ إِنِّي قُمْتُ بَعْدَ رَوَاحِ الْجَارِيَةِ وَذَهَبْتُ إِلَى دَارِي الثَّانِيَةِ
sentences.tr: qāla al-jawhariyyu thumma innī qumtu baʿda rawāḥi al-jāriyati wa-dhahabtu ilā dārī al-thāniyati
sentences.l: Said the jeweller: Then I rose after the going of the slave-girl and went to my-house, the second,
sentences.i: The jeweller said: When the girl had gone I rose and went to my second house,
sentences.n: qāla al-jawharī, “said the jeweller”: the tag reminds the listener whose story this is. thumma innī, the narrative opener thumma inna with the first person; innī is not translated. rawāḥ, properly “going in the evening”, here simply “departure”.

sentences.t: وَحَوَّلْتُ إِلَيْهَا مَا يَحْتَاجُ إِلَيْهِ الْحَالُ مِنَ الْآلَاتِ وَالْفُرُشِ الْفَاخِرَةِ وَ نَقَلْتُ إِلَيْهَا أَوَانِيَ الصِّينِيِّ وَالزُّجَاجِ وَالْفِضَّةِ وَالذَّهَبِ
sentences.tr: wa-ḥawwaltu ilayhā mā yaḥtāju ilayhi al-ḥālu mina al-ālāti wa-al-furushi al-fākhirati wa-naqaltu ilayhā awāniya al-ṣīniyyi wa-al-zujāji wa-al-fiḍḍati wa-al-dhahabi
sentences.l: and I-shifted to-it what the situation has-need of-it of the implements and the splendid spreads, and I-carried to-it vessels of the china and the glass and the silver and the gold,
sentences.i: moved into it all that the occasion called for, the furnishings and the costly carpets and cushions, and carried there vessels of china and of glass, of silver and of gold,
sentences.n: ḥawwala (Form II), “to shift, transfer”; its shadda is the print's own, as is the madda of الآلات. ālāt, “implements, gear”, the furnishing of a house in general; furush, plural of firāsh, “things spread to sit or lie on”, carpets, mattresses and cushions. ṣīnī, “Chinese”, used as a noun for porcelain: awānī al-ṣīnī, “vessels of china”. Again a line ends on a lone و, kept as printed.

sentences.t: وَهَيَّأْتُ جَمِيعَ مَا يَحْتَاجُ إِلَيْهِ مِنَ الْمَأْكَلِ وَالْمَشْرَبِ
sentences.tr: wa-hayyaʾtu jamīʿa mā yaḥtāju ilayhi mina al-maʾkali wa-al-mashrabi
sentences.l: and I-made-ready all of what is-needed for-it of the eating and the drinking.
sentences.i: and made ready everything that was wanted in the way of food and drink.
sentences.n: maʾkal and mashrab, “what is eaten and what is drunk”, food and drink. yaḥtāju ilayhi has no stated subject here: “all that (the occasion) needs”. The shadda and hamza of هيّأت and the hamza of المأكل are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا حَضَرَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ وَنَظَرَتْ مَا فَعَلْتُهُ أَعْجَبَهَا وَأَمَرَتْنِي بِإِحْضَارِ عَلِيِّ بْنِ بَكَّارٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ḥaḍarati al-jāriyatu wa-naẓarat mā faʿaltuhu aʿjabahā wa-amaratnī bi-iḥḍāri ʿAliyyi ibni Bakkārin
sentences.l: And when the slave-girl came and looked-at what I-had-done-it, it-pleased-her, and she-commanded-me with the bringing of ʿAlī son of Bakkār.
sentences.i: When the girl came and saw what I had done, it pleased her, and she bade me fetch ʿAlī ibn Bakkār.
sentences.n: naẓarat mā, “saw what”: naẓara takes its object directly here, where Classical prose has naẓara ilā. aʿjaba, “to please”: what pleases is the subject, the one pleased the object. amara bi-, “to order (something)”: the verb takes what is ordered through bi-, here the verbal noun iḥḍār, “bringing”.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ مَا يَحْضُرُ بِهِ إِلَاّ أَنْتَ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu mā yaḥḍuru bihi illā anta
sentences.l: So I-said: None comes with-him except you.
sentences.i: So I said, “None but you can bring him.”
sentences.n: ḥaḍara bi-, “to come with”, that is, “to bring”: bi- carries the person brought. The words, with the masculine anta, are addressed to a man, the jeweller, and so would sit more easily in the slave-girl's mouth; fa-qālat, “she said”, may have stood here; as printed the line reads fa-qultu, “I said”, perhaps the jeweller telling himself the errand is his, for he goes at once. The print's reading is kept. It sets the shadda of illā on the final alif (الاّ), and it stays there.

sentences.t: فَذَهَبْتُ إِلَيْهِ وَأَحْضَرْتُهُ عَلَى أَتَمِّ حَالٍ وَقَدْ رَاقَتْ مَحَاسِنُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-dhahabtu ilayhi wa-aḥḍartuhu ʿalā atammi ḥālin wa-qad rāqat maḥāsinuhu
sentences.l: So I-went to-him and brought-him in the most-complete of state, his-beauties having-grown-clear.
sentences.i: So I went to him and brought him back in the best of trim, his good looks bright and fresh again.
sentences.n: ʿalā atammi ḥālin, “in the most perfect of states”: an elative before an indefinite noun. rāqa, “to be clear, limpid”, of water or wine, hence “to be bright and pleasing”: the beauty that love-sickness had clouded has cleared. maḥāsin, “good points, charms”, a plural used for good looks. The shadda of اتمّ is the print's own.

sentences.t: قَالَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ فَتَلَقَّيْتُهُ وَتَرَحَّبْتُ بِهِ ثُمَّ أَجْلَسْتُهُ عَلَى مَرْتَبَةٍ تَصْلُحُ لَهُ وَوَضَعْتُ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ شَيْأً مِنَ الْمَشْمُومِ الْمُنَزَّةِ فِي بَعْضِ الْأَوَانِي الصِّينِيِّ وَالْبَلُّورِ مِنْ سَائِرِ الْأَلْوَانِ
sentences.tr: qāla al-jawhariyyu fa-talaqqaytuhu wa-taraḥḥabtu bihi thumma ajlastuhu ʿalā martabatin taṣluḥu lahu wa-waḍaʿtu bayna yadayhi shayʾan mina al-mashmūmi al-munazzahi fī baʿḍi al-awānī al-ṣīniyyi wa-al-ballūri min sāʾiri al-alwāni
sentences.l: Said the jeweller: So I-met-him and bade-welcome to-him, then I-seated-him on a cushioned-seat befitting for-him, and I-set between his-two-hands something of the smelled-things, the choice, in some of the vessels, the china and the crystal, of all the colours.
sentences.i: The jeweller said: I went out to meet him and made him welcome, seated him on a couch worthy of him, and set before him choice sweet-smelling flowers in vessels of china and crystal of every colour.
sentences.n: taraḥḥaba bi- (Form V), “to bid welcome”, to say marḥaban to someone: bi- marks the guest. martaba, “a raised, cushioned seat”. bayna yadayhi, “between his two hands”, is “before him”. mashmūm, “what is smelled”: flowers and sweet herbs. المنزة is read as al-munazzah, “kept pure, choice”, the print writing ة for final ه; the reading is the likeliest, not certain. al-ṣīnī stands beside al-awānī without the feminine agreement Classical would want (al-ṣīniyya), or is taken as a noun, “china”. ballūr, “crystal”. sāʾir, “the whole, every”; its hamza is the print's own.

sentences.t: وَوَضَعْتُ سُفْرَةً فِيهَا مِنْ سَائِرِ الْأَلْوَانِ الْمُلَوَّنَةِ مِمَّا تَشْرَحُ رُؤْيَتُهُ الصَّدْرَ وَجَلَسْتُ أُحَدِّثُهُ وَأُسَلِّيهِ
sentences.tr: wa-waḍaʿtu sufratan fīhā min sāʾiri al-alwāni al-mulawwanati mimmā tashraḥu ruʾyatuhu al-ṣadra wa-jalastu uḥaddithuhu wa-usallīhi
sentences.l: And I-set a food-cloth, in-it of all the colours, the coloured, of-what its-sight opens the breast; and I-sat talking-to-him and diverting-him.
sentences.i: Then I laid a spread with dishes of every kind and colour, such as gladden the heart to look upon, and sat talking with him and keeping him amused.
sentences.n: sufra, “a food-mat, a spread table”. alwān, “colours”, is also the ordinary word for “dishes, courses”, and the text plays on both: al-alwān al-mulawwana, “the coloured dishes”, dishes of every hue; min is partitive, “some of”. sharaḥa al-ṣadr, “to open the breast”, is “to gladden”; ruʾyatuhu, “the seeing of it”, is its subject (printed رويته, without the hamza). uḥaddithuhu wa-usallīhi, two imperfects describing how he sat: “talking to him and cheering him”. The shadda of الملوّنة is the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْجَارِيَةَ مَضَتْ وَغَابَتْ إِلَى الْمَسَاءِ وَعَادَتْ بَعْدَ الْمَغْرِبِ وَمَعَهَا شَمْسُ النَّهَارِ وَوَصِيفَتَانِ لَاغَيْرُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-jāriyata maḍat wa-ghābat ilā al-masāʾi wa-ʿādat baʿda al-maghribi wa-maʿahā Shamsu al-Nahāri wa-waṣīfatāni lā ghayru
sentences.l: Then the slave-girl went-off and was-absent until the evening, and returned after the sunset, with-her Shams al-Nahār and two-waiting-maids, no other.
sentences.i: Then the girl went away and stayed away until evening, and came back after sunset, bringing Shams al-Nahār and two waiting-maids, no more.
sentences.n: maghrib, “the place or time of sunset”, also the sunset prayer. waṣīfa, “maid-servant, young serving-woman”; waṣīfatāni is the dual. lā ghayru, “and none other, only”: ghayr cut off from what it governs takes a bare ḍamma; the print runs the two words together (لاغير). The hamza of المساء is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَتْ عَلِيَّ بْنَ بَكَّارٍ وَرَآهَا قَامَ قَائِمًا وَاعْتَنَقَهَا فَاعْتَنَقَتْهُ الْأُخْرَى فَسَقَطَا عَلَى الْأَرْضِ مَغْشِيًّا عَلَيْهِمَا قَدْرَ سَاعَةٍ زَمَانِيَّةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾat ʿAliyya ibna Bakkārin wa-raʾāhā qāma qāʾiman wa-iʿtanaqahā fa-iʿtanaqathu al-ukhrā fa-saqaṭā ʿalā al-arḍi maghshiyyan ʿalayhimā qadra sāʿatin zamāniyyatin
sentences.l: And when she-saw ʿAlī son of Bakkār and he-saw-her, he-rose standing and embraced-her, and the other embraced-him, and they-two-fell on the ground, swooned upon-them-two, the measure of an hour of time.
sentences.i: When she saw ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and he saw her, he sprang to his feet and threw his arms about her, and she clasped him in turn; and the two of them fell to the ground in a swoon, and lay so for the space of a full hour.
sentences.n: qāma qāʾiman, “he rose up standing”: the participle repeats the verb for emphasis. al-ukhrā, “the other (woman)”, means simply “she in her turn”. maghshiyyan ʿalayhimā, “in a swoon”: ghushiya ʿalayhi, “he was overcome (by a faint)”, is impersonal, so the participle stays singular and the dual sits in the pronoun. qadra sāʿatin zamāniyyatin, “the measure of an hour of time”, an accusative of extent; zamānī, “of time”, insists on a true hour. The hamzas of رأت and قائما and the madda of رآها are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَفَاقَا أَقْبَلَا عَلَى بَعْضِهِمَا يَتَشَاكَيَانِ أَلَمَ الْفِرَاقِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā afāqā aqbalā ʿalā baʿḍihimā yatashākayāni alama al-firāqi
sentences.l: And when they-two-came-to, they-two-turned towards each-other, complaining-to-one-another (of) the pain of the parting.
sentences.i: When they came to themselves, they turned to each other and poured out to one another the pain of their parting.
sentences.n: afāqa, “to come round, recover one's senses”. aqbala ʿalā, “to turn towards, give oneself to”. ʿalā baʿḍihimā, “to each other”: baʿḍ with the pronoun for “one another” is a post-Classical turn. yatashākayāni (Form VI, dual), “complaining to each other”, describes how they turned.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ جَلَسَا يَتَحَدَّثَانِ بِكَلَامٍ فَصِيحٍ عَذْبٍ رَقِيقٍ وَاسْتَعْمَلَا شَيْأً مِنَ الطِّيبِ
sentences.tr: thumma jalasā yataḥaddathāni bi-kalāmin faṣīḥin ʿadhbin raqīqin wa-istaʿmalā shayʾan mina al-ṭībi
sentences.l: Then they-two-sat conversing with speech eloquent, sweet, tender, and they-two-used something of the perfume.
sentences.i: Then they sat and talked together in words eloquent, sweet and tender, and put on a little perfume.
sentences.n: taḥaddatha bi-, “to talk in (a manner of speech)”: bi- names the words used. ṭīb, “perfume, scent”; istaʿmala (Form X), “to make use of”. The shadda and the closing kasra of يتحدّثانِ are the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمَا صَارَا يَشْكُرَانِ مِنْ صُنْعِي مَعَهُمَا
sentences.tr: thumma innahumā ṣārā yashkurāni min ṣunʿī maʿahumā
sentences.l: Then they-two began thanking (me) from my-doing with-them-two.
sentences.i: Then they began to thank me for what I had done for them.
sentences.n: ṣāra with an imperfect, “to begin to”, a common Middle Arabic auxiliary. shakara min, “to thank for”: Classical says shakara ʿalā; here min gives the ground of the thanks. ṣunʿ, “a deed, a kindness done”; ṣunʿī maʿahumā, “my doing with them”, the good turn I did them.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهُمَا هَلْ لَكُمَا فِي شَيْءٍ مِنَ الطَّعَامِ فَقَالَا نَعَمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahumā hal lakumā fī shayʾin mina al-ṭaʿāmi fa-qālā naʿam
sentences.l: So I-said to-them-two: Is there for-you-two (a desire) in something of the food? And they-two-said: Yes.
sentences.i: So I said to them, “Would you care for something to eat?” “Yes,” they said.
sentences.n: hal lakumā fī, “have you two a mind for”: la- marks whose the wish is, and fī names the thing wished for. Here the print writes شيء in full, with its hamza, after شيأ above.

sentences.t: فَأَحْضَرْتُ شَيْأً مِنَ الطَّعَامِ فَأَكَلَا حَتَّى اكْتَفَيَا ثُمَّ غَسَلَا أَيْدِيَهُمَا
sentences.tr: fa-aḥḍartu shayʾan mina al-ṭaʿāmi fa-akalā ḥattā iktafayā thumma ghasalā aydiyahumā
sentences.l: So I-brought a-thing of the food, and they-two-ate until they-two-had-enough; then they-two-washed their-two hands.
sentences.i: So I brought them something to eat, and they ate until they had had their fill; then they washed their hands.
sentences.n: The jeweller is still telling the tale. shayʾ, “a thing, something”, is spelled here شيأ, with its hamza seated on an alif, as the accusative shayʾan; the hamza is the print's own, as is the ḍamma of فأحضرتُ. The verbs are dual, for the two lovers: akalā, iktafayā (Form VIII of kafā, “to have enough”), ghasalā. aydī is the plural of yad, “hand”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ نَقَلْتُهُمَا إِلَى مَجْلِسٍ آخَرَ وَأَحْضَرْتُ لَهُمَا الشَّرَابَ فَشَرِبَا وَسَكِرَا وَمَالَا عَلَى بَعْضِهِمَا
sentences.tr: thumma naqaltuhumā ilā majlisin ākhara wa-aḥḍartu lahumā al-sharāba fa-sharibā wa-sakirā wa-mālā ʿalā baʿḍihimā
sentences.l: Then I-moved-them-two to another sitting-room and brought for-them-two the drink; and they-two-drank and became-drunk and leaned upon each-other-of-them-two.
sentences.i: Then I took them into another room and set wine before them, and they drank until they were drunk and leaned against one another.
sentences.n: majlis, “a place of sitting”, is a reception room. al-sharāb, “the drink”, is wine, as sakirā, “they became drunk”, makes plain. māla ʿalā, “to lean on”; ʿalā baʿḍihimā, “upon one another”, is the everyday reciprocal, where Classical usage would set it out in full as baʿḍuhumā ʿalā baʿḍin. ākhar, “other”, takes no tanwīn. The madda of آخر and the ḍammas of نقلتُهما and وأحضرتُ are the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ شَمْسَ النَّهَارِ قَالَتْ لِي يَا سَيِّدِي كَمِّلْ جَمِيلَكَ وَأَحْضِرْ لَنَا عُودًا أَوْ شَيْأً مِنْ آلَاتِ الطَّرَبِ لِأَجْلِ أَنْ يَكْمُلَ سُرُورُنَا فِي هَذِهِ السَّاعَةِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna Shamsa al-Nahāri qālat lī yā sayyidī kammil jamīlaka wa-aḥḍir lanā ʿūdan aw shayʾan min ālāti al-ṭarabi li-ajli an yakmula surūrunā fī hādhihi al-sāʿati
sentences.l: Then (indeed) Shams al-Nahār said to-me: O my-master, complete your-kindness, and bring for-us a-lute or some-thing of the instruments of rapture, for-the-sake-of that our-joy be-complete in this hour.
sentences.i: Then Shams al-Nahār said to me, “Sir, crown your kindness: bring us a lute, or some other instrument of music, so that our happiness may be complete this hour.”
sentences.n: kammil, the imperative of Form II, “make complete”; its kasra and shadda are the print's own. jamīl, “a kindness, a good turn”. ʿūd, “the lute”. ṭarab is the rapture that music stirs, so ālāt al-ṭarab, “instruments of rapture”, are musical instruments; the madda of آلات is the print's. li-ajli an, “for the sake of”, “so that”, takes the subjunctive yakmula. yā sayyidī, “my master”, is courtesy here, “sir”.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ عَلَى الرَّأْسِ وَالْعَيْنِ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu ʿalā al-raʾsi wa-al-ʿayni
sentences.l: So I-said: Upon the head and the eye.
sentences.i: “On my head and my eyes be it,” I said.
sentences.n: A set formula of willing service: the thing asked is taken up as a charge laid on one's head and eyes. The hamza of الرأس is the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنِّي قُمْتُ وَأَحْضَرْتُ عُودًا فَأَخَذَتْهُ وَأَصْلَحَتْهُ
sentences.tr: thumma innī qumtu wa-aḥḍartu ʿūdan fa-akhadhathu wa-aṣlaḥathu
sentences.l: Then (indeed) I rose and brought a-lute; and she-took-it and put-it-right.
sentences.i: So I rose and brought a lute, and she took it and tuned it.
sentences.n: The print has واصحلته, a misprint for واصلحته, corrected here. aṣlaḥa (Form IV), “to put in order, set right”, said of a lute means to tune it. thumma innī, like thumma inna, only opens the clause. The sukūn of فأخذتْه is the print's own: it marks the feminine ending, akhadhat-hu, “she took it”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا وَضَعَتْهُ فِي حِجْرِهَا وَضَرَبَتْ عَلَيْهِ ضَرْبًا بَلِيغًا هَيَّجَتِ الشُّجُونَ وَأَطْرَبَتِ الْمَحْزُونَ ثُمَّ أَنْشَدَتْ هَذَيْنِ الْبَيْتَيْنِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahā waḍaʿathu fī ḥijrihā wa-ḍarabat ʿalayhi ḍarban balīghan hayyajati al-shujūna wa-aṭrabati al-maḥzūna thumma anshadat hādhayni al-baytayni
sentences.l: Then (indeed) she laid-it in her-lap and struck upon-it a-striking far-reaching: it-stirred-up the sorrows and enraptured the grieving-one; then she-recited these two verses:
sentences.i: Then she laid it in her lap and played upon it with such mastery that she stirred up every sorrow and filled the sorrowful with delight; and then she recited these two lines:
sentences.n: ḍaraba ʿalā, “to strike upon”, is to play a stringed instrument; ḍarban balīghan, an absolute object, “a playing that reached its mark”, from balīgh, “far-reaching, eloquent”. The two clauses after it rhyme (sajʿ): hayyajat al-shujūn / aṭrabat al-maḥzūn. shujūn, “cares, sorrows”; aṭraba (Form IV), “to move to ṭarab, to enrapture”. anshada, “to recite verse”; hādhayni al-baytayni is dual and accusative, “these two lines”.

sentences.t:
اَرِقْتُ حَتَّى كَأَنِّيْ اَعْشِقُ الْاَرِقَا * وَذُبْتُ حَتَّى كَأَنَّ السُّقْمَ لِي خُلقَا
وَفَاضَ دَمْعِي عَلَى خَدِّي فَاَحْرَقَهُ * يَا لَيْتَ شِعْرِي هَلْ بَعْدَ الْفِرَاقِ لِقَا
sentences.tr:
ariqtu ḥattā kaʾannī aʿshiqu al-ariqā * wa-dhubtu ḥattā kaʾanna al-suqma lī khuluqā
wa-fāḍa damʿī ʿalā khaddī fa-aḥraqahu * yā layta shiʿrī hal baʿda al-firāqi liqā
sentences.l:
I-lay-sleepless until as-if I love the sleepless-one, * and I-melted until as-if the sickness (were) to-me a-nature;
and my-tears overflowed upon my-cheek and burned-it: * O would-that my-knowing — is-there after the parting a-meeting?
sentences.i:
I have lain awake until it seems I love the wakeful, * and wasted until it seems that sickness is my nature;
my tears have flooded down my cheek and scorched it — * would that I knew: after parting, is there meeting?
sentences.n: ariqa, “to lie sleepless”. The print points the first rhyme word al-ariqā, “the sleepless one”; the sense may rather want al-araqa, “sleeplessness” (“as if I were in love with wakefulness”), a difference of one vowel. It also gives aʿshiqu a kasra where the verb ʿashiqa, yaʿshaqu has a fatḥa. Both are kept as printed. dhāba, “to melt”, is said of a lover wasting away; khuluq, “inborn character”. yā layta shiʿrī, “would that my knowing (were)”, is the set phrase for “I wonder”. liqā is liqāʾ, “meeting”, its hamza dropped for the rhyme in -qā; the closing alif of each rhyme word is the lengthened vowel of the rhyme.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا أَخَذَتْ فِي غِنَاءِ الْأَشْعَارِ حَتَّى حَيَّرَتِ الْأَفْكَارَ وَهِيَ تُغَنِّي بِأَصْوَاتٍ مُخْتَلِفَةٍ وَأَشْعَارٍ رَائِقَةٍ حَتَّى كَادَ الْمَجْلِسُ أَنْ يَرْقُصَ مِنْ شِدَّةِ الطَّرَبِ بِمَا أَتَتْ فِيهِ مِنْ مَغَانِيهَا بِالْعَجَبِ وَمَا بَقِيَ لَنَا عَقْلٌ وَلَافِكْرٌ
sentences.tr: thumma innahā akhadhat fī ghināʾi al-ashʿāri ḥattā ḥayyarati al-afkāra wa-hiya tughannī bi-aṣwātin mukhtalifatin wa-ashʿārin rāʾiqatin ḥattā kāda al-majlisu an yarquṣa min shiddati al-ṭarabi bi-mā atat fīhi min maghānīhā bi-al-ʿajabi wa-mā baqiya lanā ʿaqlun wa-lā fikrun
sentences.l: Then (indeed) she took-to the singing of the poems until she-bewildered the thoughts, she singing in voices varied and poems limpid, until the sitting-room was-about to dance from the intensity of the rapture, by-reason-of what she-came in-it of her-songs with the wonder; and there-remained not to-us mind nor thought.
sentences.i: Then she fell to singing poem after poem until every thought was bewildered, singing in changing strains and lovely verses, till the very room was ready to dance for sheer rapture at the wonders she worked in her songs; and we were left with neither wit nor reason.
sentences.n: akhadha fī, “to set about, begin”. al-ashʿār and al-afkār rhyme (sajʿ). rāʾiq, “clear, limpid”, of verse “fine, pleasing”. kāda … an yarquṣa, “was about to dance”: the an before the subjunctive is usual in this text, where the strictest Classical usage leaves it out after kāda. bi-mā atat fīhi min maghānīhā bi-al-ʿajabi is loosely built: the first bi- gives the cause, “because of what”, and atā bi-, “to come with”, is “to produce”, so the clause means “for the wonders she produced in her songs”, with the verb's bi- placed at the end. maghānī, “songs, melodies”. The print runs wa-lā fikr together as ولافكر. The shadda of تغنّي and the hamza of غناء and رائقة are its own.

sentences.t: وَلَمَّا اسْتَقَرَّ بِنَا الْجُلُوسُ وَدَارَتْ بَيْنَنَا الْكُؤُسُ أَطْرَبَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ بِالنَّغَمَاتِ وَأَنْشَدَتْ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: wa-lammā istaqarra binā al-julūsu wa-dārat baynanā al-kuʾūsu aṭrabati al-jāriyatu bi-al-naghamāti wa-anshadat hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And when the sitting settled with-us and the cups went-round between-us, the slave-girl enraptured (us) with the melodies and recited these verses:
sentences.i: And when we were settled in our seats and the cups were going round among us, the slave-girl ravished us with her melodies and recited these lines:
sentences.n: al-julūs and al-kuʾūs rhyme (sajʿ). istaqarra bi-, “to settle with”: “the sitting settled with us”, we were settled in our places. al-kuʾūs, “the cups”, plural of kaʾs, is printed الكؤس, with one wāw where the fuller spelling is كؤوس; the hamza is the print's own, as are the shaddas of ولمّا and استقرّ. al-jāriya, “the slave-girl”, is not named: the text does not say whether she is Shams al-Nahār's confidante or Shams al-Nahār herself, who has been playing; aṭraba is left without an object, “delighted (us)”.

sentences.t:
وَعَدَ الْحَبِيْبُ بِوَصْلِهِ وَوَفَى لِيْ * فِيْ لَيْلَةٍ سَأُعُدُّهَا بِلَيَالِيْ
يَا لَيْلَةً سَمَحَ الزَّمَانُ لَنَا بِهَا * فِيْ غَفْلَةِ الْوَاشِيْنَ وَالْعُذَّال
بَاتَ الْحَبِيْبُ يَضُمُّنِي بِيَمِيْنِهِ * مِنْ فَرْحَتِى فَضَمَمْتُهُ بِشِمَالِيْ
عَانَقْتُهُ وَرَشَفْتُ خُمْرَةَ رِيقِهِ * وَحَظِيْتُ بِالْمَعْسُوْلِ وَالْعُسَّالِ
sentences.tr:
waʿada al-ḥabību bi-waṣlihi wa-wafā lī * fī laylatin saʾuʿudduhā bi-layālī
yā laylatan samaḥa al-zamānu lanā bihā * fī ghaflati al-wāshīna wa-al-ʿudhdhāli
bāta al-ḥabību yaḍummunī bi-yamīnihi * min farḥatī fa-ḍamamtuhu bi-shimālī
ʿānaqtuhu wa-rashaftu khumrata rīqihi * wa-ḥaẓītu bi-al-maʿsūli wa-al-ʿussāli
sentences.i:
My love promised to come to me, and kept his word, * one night that I shall count as many nights.
O night that Time bestowed on us * while slanderers and censurers slept!
All night my love held me close in his right arm, * and in my joy I held him with my left;
I embraced him and sipped the wine of his mouth, * and had my fill of the honey and its gatherers.
sentences.n: As is the rule in Arabic love poetry, the beloved is masculine (al-ḥabīb, -hu) whoever is meant. waṣl, “union”, the lovers' meeting; wafā, “to keep faith”. saʾuʿudduhā, “I shall count it”, is printed with a ḍamma on the hamza where the verb ʿadda has saʾaʿudduhā; kept as printed. samaḥa bi-, “to grant, be generous with”: the verb takes its gift with bi-, bihā, “(granted us) it”. wāshūn, “slanderers, talebearers”, and ʿudhdhāl, “censurers”, are the lovers' stock enemies; the print leaves the case vowel off العذّال. bāta, “to spend the night”. rīq is saliva, the lover's mouth. The print points خمرة with a ḍamma, khumra, “ferment, the aroma of wine”, where khamra, “wine”, is likelier; kept as printed. al-maʿsūl, “the honeyed”; al-ʿussāl as printed is a plural, “honey-gatherers”, and its sense here is uncertain: perhaps “the honey and its maker”, both the beloved, with the word chosen for the rhyme. The long vowels marked with sukūn (لِيْ، فِيْ) are the print's style.

sentences.t: قَالَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ فَبَيْنَمَا نَحْنُ فِي بَحْرِ السُّرُورِ غَارِقُونَ وَإِذَا بِوَصِيفَةٍ صَغِيرَةٍ دَخَلَتْ عَلَيْنَا وَهِيَ تَرْتَعِدُ
sentences.tr: qāla al-jawhariyyu fa-baynamā naḥnu fī baḥri al-surūri ghāriqūna wa-idhā bi-waṣīfatin ṣaghīratin dakhalat ʿalaynā wa-hiya tartaʿidu
sentences.l: The jeweller said: And while we (were) in the sea of joy drowning-ones, and behold, a little maid-servant came-in upon-us, she trembling,
sentences.i: The jeweller said: While we were drowned in a sea of delight, all at once a little serving-girl came in upon us, trembling,
sentences.n: The print has تي, a misprint for في, corrected here. baynamā … wa-idhā bi-, “while … and behold”: the storyteller's usual frame for an interruption; after idhā the bi- only marks what appears. waṣīfa, “young maid-servant”. wa-hiya tartaʿidu, a circumstantial clause, “while she trembled”.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ يَاسَيِّدَتِي انْظُرِي كَيْفَ تَذْهَبِينَ فَإِنَّ الْقَوْمَ أَحَاطُوا بِكُمْ وَأَدْرَكُوكُمْ وَلَمْ نَدْرِ سَبَبَ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat yā sayyidatī unẓurī kayfa tadhhabīna fa-inna al-qawma aḥāṭū bikum wa-adrakūkum wa-lam nadri sababa dhālika
sentences.l: and she-said: O my-lady, look how you-will-go, for the people have-surrounded you and have-overtaken-you, and we-do-not know the cause of that.
sentences.i: and said, “My lady, look to how you will get away, for men have surrounded you and are upon you, and we do not know why.”
sentences.n: The print runs yā and sayyidatī together (ياسيدتي). unẓurī kayfa tadhhabīna, “see how you are to go”: find a way out. al-qawm, “the people”, here an armed party. The plural “you” of bikum takes in the whole company. aḥāṭa bi- (Form IV), “to surround”, takes its object through bi-. lam nadri: the jussive of darā, “to know”, its final vowel letter dropped.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعْتُ كَلَامَهُ قُمْتُ مَرْعُوبًا وَإِذَا بِجَارِيَةٍ تَقُولُ جَاءَكُمُ الْبَلَاءُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿtu kalāmahu qumtu marʿūban wa-idhā bi-jāriyatin taqūlu jāʾakumu al-balāʾu
sentences.l: And when I-heard his-speech, I-rose terrified, and behold, a slave-girl saying: The calamity has-come-to-you!
sentences.i: When I heard this I sprang up in terror, and there was a slave-girl crying, “Disaster is upon you!”
sentences.n: kalāmahu, “his words”, though the speaker is the little maid: the print's masculine pronoun is kept, and may be a slip for kalāmahā, “her words”. The damma of سمعتُ is the print's own, marking “I heard”. jāʾakumu: the pronoun -kum takes a helping u before the article. The hamza of جاءكم is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَضَاقَتْ عَلَيَّ الْأَرْضُ بِمَا رَحُبَتْ وَنَظَرْتُ إِلَى الْبَابِ فَلَمْ أَجِدْ مَسْلَكًا فَنَطَّيْتُ إِلَى دَارِ بَعْضِ الْجِيرَانِ وَتَخَبَّيْتُ
sentences.tr: fa-ḍāqat ʿalayya al-arḍu bi-mā raḥubat wa-naẓartu ilā al-bābi fa-lam ajid maslakan fa-naṭṭaytu ilā dāri baʿḍi al-jīrāni wa-takhabbaytu
sentences.l: And the earth became-narrow upon-me with what it-was-wide, and I-looked to the door and did-not find a way-out; so I-leapt to the house of some-of the neighbours and hid-myself.
sentences.i: The earth, for all its breadth, grew narrow about me. I looked to the door and found no way out, so I leapt across into a neighbour's house and hid.
sentences.n: ḍāqat ʿalayya al-arḍu bi-mā raḥubat, “the earth grew strait upon me, wide as it was”, is a Qurʾānic phrase (9:25, 9:118) for utter helplessness; bi-mā raḥubat, “with its wideness”, means “for all its breadth”. naṭṭaytu, “I jumped”, is Middle Arabic: colloquial naṭṭa, “to leap”, conjugated as if its root ended in y (Classical would give naṭaṭtu). takhabbaytu, “I hid”, is likewise the spoken form of Classical takhabbaʾtu, its hamza turned to y. The shaddas of عليّ, نطّيت and تخبّيت are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَوَجَدْتُ النَّاسَ قَدْ دَخَلُوا دَارِي وَصَارَ لَهُمْ ضَجَّةٌ عَظِيمَةٌ
sentences.tr: fa-wajadtu al-nāsa qad dakhalū dārī wa-ṣāra lahum ḍajjatun ʿaẓīmatun
sentences.l: And I-found the people had entered my-house, and there-came-to-be to-them a great clamour.
sentences.i: There I found that men had broken into my house and were raising a great uproar.
sentences.n: The print has فرجدت, a misprint for فوجدت, corrected here. ṣāra lahum ḍajjatun, “there came to be for them an uproar”: a masculine verb with a feminine subject is allowed when the verb comes first and something stands between, and Middle Arabic does it freely.

sentences.t: فَاعْتَقَدْتُ أَنَّ خَبَرَنَا قَدْ وَصَلَ إِلَى الْخَلِيفَةِ فَأَرْسَلَ صَاحِبَ الشُّرْطَةِ لِيَكْبِسَ عَلَيْنَا وَيُحْضِرَنَا إِلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-iʿtaqadtu anna khabaranā qad waṣala ilā al-khalīfati fa-arsala ṣāḥiba al-shurṭati li-yakbisa ʿalaynā wa-yuḥḍiranā ilayhi
sentences.l: And I-believed that our-news had reached the Caliph, and he-sent the master of the police to-raid upon-us and bring-us to-him.
sentences.i: I was sure that word of us had reached the Caliph, and that he had sent the chief of police to fall upon us and bring us before him.
sentences.n: ṣāḥib al-shurṭa, “master of the police”, the city's chief of police. kabasa ʿalā, “to burst in on, raid”; li- with the subjunctive, “in order to”. The marks on ليكْبِس are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَبَقِيتُ مُتَحَيِّرًا وَلَمْ أَزَلْ مُقِيمًا إِلَى نِصْفِ اللَّيْلِ وَلَمْ أَقْدِرْ عَلَى الْخُرُوجِ مِنَ الْمَكَانِ الَّذِى أَنَا فِيهِ
sentences.tr: fa-baqītu mutaḥayyiran wa-lam azal muqīman ilā niṣfi al-layli wa-lam aqdir ʿalā al-khurūji mina al-makāni alladhī anā fīhi
sentences.l: So I-remained bewildered, and I-did-not cease staying until the middle of the night, and I-was-not-able for the going-out from the place which I (was) in-it.
sentences.i: There I stayed, at my wits' end, until midnight, unable to leave the place where I was.
sentences.n: lam azal, “I did not cease”, with its predicate in the accusative: “I went on staying”. qadara ʿalā, “to be able to”. الذى is the print's spelling of alladhī.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ صَاحِبُ الدَّارِ وَأَحَسَّ بِي فَفَزِعَ وَصَارَ عِنْدَهُ فَزَعٌ عَظِيمٌ مِنِّي فَطَلَعَ مِنْ بَيْتِهِ وَجَاءَ إِلَيَّ وَبِيَدِهِ سَيْفٌ مَسْلُولٌ وَقَالَ مَنْ هَذَا الَّذِي عِنْدَنَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāma ṣāḥibu al-dāri wa-aḥassa bī fa-faziʿa wa-ṣāra ʿindahu fazaʿun ʿaẓīmun minnī fa-ṭalaʿa min baytihi wa-jāʾa ilayya wa-bi-yadihi sayfun maslūlun wa-qāla man hādhā alladhī ʿindanā
sentences.l: Then the master of the house rose and sensed me, and took-fright, and there-came-to-be with-him a great fright of-me; so he-came-out from his-room and came to-me, and in-his-hand a drawn sword, and said: Who (is) this who (is) with-us?
sentences.i: Then the master of the house got up and became aware of me. He took fright, sorely afraid of me, and came out of his room toward me with a drawn sword in his hand, saying, “Who is this in our house?”
sentences.n: aḥassa bi- (Form IV), “to sense, become aware of”, takes its object through bi-. faziʿa … wa-ṣāra ʿindahu fazaʿun ʿaẓīmun, the verb and then its noun, “he was afraid, and a great fear came over him”: a doubling the storyteller likes. ṭalaʿa, “to come up, come out”; bayt is here the room where he slept. The shaddas of احسّ and اليّ and the hamza of جاء are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهُ أَنَا جَارُكَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ فَعَرَفَنِي وَرَجَعَ عَنِّي
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahu anā jāruka al-jawhariyyu fa-ʿarafanī wa-rajaʿa ʿannī
sentences.l: And I-said to-him: I (am) your-neighbour the jeweller. And he-knew-me and turned-back from-me.
sentences.i: “I am your neighbour the jeweller,” I told him; and he knew me and drew back.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ جَاءَ بِضَوْءٍ وَتَقَدَّمَ عِنْدِي وَقَالَ لِي يَا أَخِي مَاهَانَ عَلَيَّ الَّذِي جَرَى لَكَ اللَّيْلَةَ
sentences.tr: thumma jāʾa bi-ḍawʾin wa-taqaddama ʿindī wa-qāla lī yā akhī mā hāna ʿalayya alladhī jarā laka al-laylata
sentences.l: Then he-came with a-light and came-forward to-me, and said to-me: O my-brother, not light upon-me (is) what befell you tonight.
sentences.i: Then he brought a light, came up to me and said, “My brother, what befell you tonight weighs heavily on me.”
sentences.n: jāʾa bi-, “to come with”, that is, to bring. taqaddama ʿindī, “he came forward to me”: Middle Arabic often uses ʿinda, “at, with”, where Classical would have ilā, “to”. mā hāna ʿalayya, “it was not light upon me”, a phrase of sympathy; the print runs mā and hāna together (ماهان). al-laylata, accusative of time, “tonight”. The hamzas of جاء and ضوء and the shadda of تقدّم are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهُ يَا أَخِي عَرِّفْنِي عَنْ مَنْ كَانَ فِي دَارِي وَمَنْ دَخَلَهَا وَكَسَرَ بَابِي فَإِنِّي هَرَبْتُ عِنْدَكَ وَلَمْ أَعْلَمِ الْقِصَّةَ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahu yā akhī ʿarrifnī ʿan man kāna fī dārī wa-man dakhalahā wa-kasara bābī fa-innī harabtu ʿindaka wa-lam aʿlami al-qiṣṣata
sentences.l: And I-said to-him: O my-brother, make-me-know about who was in my-house, and who entered-it and broke my-door; for I fled to-you and did-not know the story.
sentences.i: “My brother,” I said, “tell me who was in my house, who broke my door and went in; I fled to you and know nothing of what happened.”
sentences.n: The print has احي, a misprint for اخي, corrected here. ʿarrifnī (Form II imperative), “inform me”; ʿan man, “about whom”, is set as two words where Classical spelling joins them (عمّن). harabtu ʿindaka, “I fled to you”: ʿinda again for ilā. lam aʿlami: the jussive takes a helping i before the article. The shadda of عرّفني is the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لِي إِنَّ اللُّصُوصَ الَّذِينَ جَاؤُا إِلَى جِيرَانِنَا بِالْأَمْسِ وَقَتَلُوا فُلَانًا وَأَخَذُوا مَالَهُ قَدْ رَأَوْكَ بِالْأَمْسِ وَأَنْتَ تَنْقُلُ حَوَائِجَكَ وَتَأْتِي بِهَا إِلَى هَذَا الْمَكَانِ فَجَاؤُكَ وَأَخَذُوا مَا عِنْدَكَ وَقَتَلُوا ضُيُوفَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lī inna al-luṣūṣa alladhīna jāʾū ilā jīrāninā bi-al-amsi wa-qatalū fulānan wa-akhadhū mālahu qad raʾawka bi-al-amsi wa-anta tanqulu ḥawāʾijaka wa-taʾtī bihā ilā hādhā al-makāni fa-jāʾūka wa-akhadhū mā ʿindaka wa-qatalū ḍuyūfaka
sentences.l: And he-said to-me: The thieves who came to our-neighbours yesterday and killed So-and-so and took his-wealth had-seen-you yesterday, you moving your-things and bringing them to this place; so they-came-to-you, and took what (was) with-you, and killed your-guests.
sentences.i: He said to me, “The thieves who came to our neighbours yesterday, killed So-and-so and took his money, saw you yesterday carrying your things over and bringing them here. So they came for you, took all you had, and killed your guests.”
sentences.n: bi-al-amsi, “yesterday”: bi- here is “in, at” of time. fulān, “So-and-so”, stands in for a name the speaker does not need to give. ḥawāʾij, “needs”, then “belongings, things”. atā bi-, “to bring”: taʾtī bihā, “bringing them”. جاؤا and فجاؤك (jāʾū, jāʾūka) are an older way of writing the hamza of the plural verb; the hamzas of these and of رأوك and حوائجك are the print's own.

sentences.t: قَالَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ فَقُمْتُ أَنَا وَجَارِي وَجِئْنَا إِلَى الدَّارِ فَوَجَدْنَاهَا خَالِيَةً وَلَمْ يَبْقَ فِيهَا شَيْءٌ
sentences.tr: qāla al-jawhariyyu fa-qumtu anā wa-jārī wa-jiʾnā ilā al-dāri fa-wajadnāhā khāliyatan wa-lam yabqa fīhā shayʾun
sentences.l: The jeweller said: So I rose, I and my-neighbour, and we-came to the house, and found-it empty, and there-did-not remain in-it a-thing.
sentences.i: The jeweller said: So my neighbour and I got up and went to the house, and we found it empty; nothing was left in it.
sentences.n: qumtu anā wa-jārī: to add a second subject to “I rose”, Arabic first repeats the pronoun, anā. lam yabqa, the jussive of baqiya, “to remain”. The hamzas of جئنا and شيء are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَتَحَيَّرْتُ فِي أَمْرِي وَقُلْتُ أَمَّا الْأَمْتِعَةُ فَلَا أُبَالِي بِضَيَاعِهَا وَإِنْ كُنْتُ اسْتَعَرْتُ بَعْضَ الْأَمْتِعَةِ مِنْ أَصْحَابِي وَضَاعَتْ فَلَابَأْسَ بِذَلِكَ لِأَنَّهُمْ عَرَفُوا عُذْرِي بِذَهَابِ مَالِي وَنَهْبِ دَارِي
sentences.tr: fa-taḥayyartu fī amrī wa-qultu ammā al-amtiʿatu fa-lā ubālī bi-ḍayāʿihā wa-in kuntu istaʿartu baʿḍa al-amtiʿati min aṣḥābī wa-ḍāʿat fa-lā baʾsa bi-dhālika li-annahum ʿarafū ʿudhrī bi-dhahābi mālī wa-nahbi dārī
sentences.l: And I-was-bewildered in my-affair, and I-said: As for the goods, I-do-not care about their-loss; and if I-had borrowed some-of the goods from my-friends and they-were-lost, there-is-no harm in that, because they-know my-excuse by-the-going of my-wealth and the plundering of my-house.
sentences.i: I did not know what to do, and I said to myself, “The goods I do not mind losing; and if some of them were borrowed from my friends and are gone, no matter: they will accept my excuse, with my own money gone and my house plundered.
sentences.n: ammā … fa-, “as for … (then)”: the fa- marks the main clause. bālā bi-, “to care about”, takes its object through bi-: lā ubālī bi-ḍayāʿihā, “I care nothing for their loss”. The print runs lā and baʾs together (لاباس) and writes baʾs without its hamza: lā baʾsa bi-dhālika, “there is no harm in that”. ʿarafū, a past tense, states a certainty: “they will know (and accept)”. bi-dhahābi mālī, “through the going of my money”.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا عَلِيُّ بْنُ بَكَّارٍ وَمَحْظِيَّةُ أَمِيرِ الْمُؤْمِنِينَ فَأَخْشَى أَنْ يَشْتَهِرَ الْأَمْرُ بَيْنَهُمَا فَيَكُونَ ذَلِكَ سَبَبَ رَوَاحِ رُوحِي
sentences.tr: wa-ammā ʿAliyyu ibnu Bakkārin wa-maḥẓiyyatu amīri al-muʾminīna fa-akhshā an yashtahira al-amru baynahumā fa-yakūna dhālika sababa rawāḥi rūḥī
sentences.l: But as for ʿAlī son of Bakkār and the favourite of the Commander of the Faithful, I-fear that the affair between-the-two-of-them become-known, and that be the cause of the going of my-soul.
sentences.i: But as for ʿAlī ibn Bakkār and the favourite of the Commander of the Faithful, I fear the affair between them will come out, and that will be the death of me.”
sentences.n: maḥẓiyya, “favoured one”, a concubine high in her master's favour; amīr al-muʾminīn, “Commander of the Faithful”, the Caliph's title. fa-yakūna, subjunctive, is still governed by an: “and that it be”. rawāḥ rūḥī, “the going of my soul”, my death, with a jingle between rawāḥ, “departure”, and rūḥ, “soul”. The hamza of المؤمنين is the print's own.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ الْتَفَتُّ إِلَى جَارِي وَقُلْتُ لَهُ أَنْتَ أَخِي وَجَارِي وَتَسْتُرُ عَلَيَّ عَوْرَاتِي فَمَا الَّذِي تُشِيرُ بِهِ عَلَيَّ مِنَ الْأُمُورِ
sentences.tr: thumma iltafattu ilā jārī wa-qultu lahu anta akhī wa-jārī wa-tasturu ʿalayya ʿawrātī fa-mā alladhī tushīru bihi ʿalayya mina al-umūri
sentences.l: Then I-turned to my-neighbour and said to-him: You (are) my-brother and my-neighbour, and you-cover over-me my-shames; so what (is) that-which you-point with-it upon-me of the matters?
sentences.i: Then I turned to my neighbour and said, “You are my brother and my neighbour, and you keep my secrets covered. What do you advise me to do?”
sentences.n: iltafattu, “I turned”: the t of the root and the t of “I” merge into one doubled letter. satara ʿalā, “to cover up (faults) for someone”. ʿawrāt, “things that must be hidden”: nakedness, then any weakness or secret that would shame one. ashāra ʿalā … bi-, “to advise someone of something”: the person advised takes ʿalā, the advice bi-, so mā alladhī tushīru bihi ʿalayya is “what is it you advise me?” The shaddas of عليّ are the print's own.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لِيَ الرَّجُلُ الَّذِي أُشِيرُ بِهِ عَلَيْكَ أَنْ تَتَرَبَّصَ فَإِنَّ الَّذِينَ دَخَلُوا دَارَكَ وَأَخَذُوا مَتَاعَكَ قَدْ قَتَلُوا أَحْسَنَ جَمَاعَةٍ مِنْ دَارِ الْخَلِيفَةِ وَقَتَلُوا جَمَاعَةً مِنْ عِنْدِ صَاحِبِ الشُّرْطَةِ وَأَعْوَانُ الدَّوْلَةِ يَدُورُونَ عَلَيْهِمْ فِي جَمِيعِ الطُّرُقِ فَلَعَلَّهُمْ يَصْدِفُوهُمْ فَيَحْصُلَ مُرَادُكَ بِغَيْرِ سَعْيٍ مِنْكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla liya al-rajulu alladhī ushīru bihi ʿalayka an tatarabbaṣa fa-inna alladhīna dakhalū dāraka wa-akhadhū matāʿaka qad qatalū aḥsana jamāʿatin min dāri al-khalīfati wa-qatalū jamāʿatan min ʿindi ṣāḥibi al-shurṭati wa-aʿwānu al-dawlati yadūrūna ʿalayhim fī jamīʿi al-ṭuruqi fa-laʿallahum yaṣdifūhum fa-yaḥṣula murāduka bi-ghayri saʿyin minka
sentences.l: And the man said to-me: That-which I-advise you of-it (is) that you-wait; for those who entered your-house and took your-goods have killed the finest company from the house of the Caliph, and killed a company from with the master of the police; and the helpers of the state are going-round after-them in all the roads, so perhaps they come-upon-them, and your-aim come-about without striving from-you.
sentences.i: The man said to me, “My advice to you is to bide your time. The men who broke into your house and took your goods have killed a band of the Caliph's household, the finest of men, and killed others of the police chief's men besides; the officers of the state are hunting them down in every street. Perhaps they will come upon them, and you will have your wish without lifting a finger.”
sentences.n: lī, “to me”, takes a helping a before the article: liya al-rajulu. tarabbaṣa (Form V), “to wait and watch, bide one's time”. aḥsana jamāʿatin, “the finest of companies”, an elative before an indefinite noun; the phrase is odd here, and the print may be at fault, but no likely correction suggests itself, so it is read as printed; dār al-khalīfa, “the Caliph's house”, his palace and household. aʿwān al-dawla, “the helpers of the state”, its officers and men; dāra ʿalā, “to go round after, hunt for”. yaṣdifūhum, “they will come upon them”, is Middle Arabic twice over: ṣadafa in this sense is colloquial (Classical says ṣādafa, Form III), and the verb has lost the -na of the indicative (yaṣdifūnahum) with nothing to cut it, a common habit of the Nights. fa-yaḥṣula, subjunctive after a fa- that answers a hope.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ الْجَوْهَرِيُّ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ رَجَعَ إِلَى دَارِهِ الثَّانِيَةِ الَّتِي هُوَ سَاكِنٌ بِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa al-jawhariyyu hādhā al-kalāma rajaʿa ilā dārihi al-thāniyati allatī huwa sākinun bihā
sentences.l: And when the jeweller heard this speech, he-returned to his-house, the second (= the other), which he (is) dwelling in-it.
sentences.i: When the jeweller heard this, he went back to his other house, the one he lived in.
sentences.n: The jeweller's “I” gives way here to “the jeweller” in the third person, as Shahrazād takes the thread back for the night's end. dārihi al-thāniya, literally “his second house”; but it was the house he called his second that he fitted out for the lovers and that the thieves stripped, so al-thāniya most likely means “the other (of the two)” here, the house he lived in, as the relative clause says. The print's word is kept. sākinun bihā, “dwelling in it”: bi- here is “in”.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka Shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she-fell-silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: And morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the speech allowed her.
sentences.n: The object comes before the subject: Shahrazāda is the one overtaken, al-ṣabāḥu the morning that overtakes. al-kalām al-mubāḥ, “the permitted speech”, the talk allowed her until dawn; the rhyme ṣabāḥ / mubāḥ closes every night.
